passage:
The leak had taken Jamal's contact list, and he knew his relatives in three countries would be next. On Saturday morning in Melbourne, before his tea went cold, he wrote in the family group: "My contacts were in a data leak. If a message comes from me or anyone asking for money, a code or a quick favour, please don't reply. Ring me instead."

Then he phoned his grandmother, who did not use the group, and read it to her slowly. He asked her to tell Aunty Sofia's household the same.

By noon his cousin Tuan wrote back, "Got a weird message from 'you' an hour ago. Ignored it. Good thing you warned us." Jamal felt his shoulders drop.

qa.q: Who did Jamal phone after posting in the family group?
qa.a: His grandmother, who did not use the group.

qa.q: What was Jamal feeling when Tuan's reply arrived?
qa.a: Jamal felt relieved, shown by his shoulders dropping when he learned the warning had come in time.

qa.q: What else could Jamal do for relatives who might still fall for a message, and why?
qa.a: Jamal could agree on a family code word to check that a request is really from him, because a shared check makes fake requests easy to spot.

qa.q: How might Tuan see the suspicious message once Jamal's warning arrived?
qa.a: Tuan probably felt confident to ignore it, since the warning made the strange message obviously suspect instead of confusing.

grounding: Because contact lists were part of the leak, the person tells relatives to ignore suspicious messages asking for money or codes.

In the hostel common room, Sarita pulled her chair close to the plug point and read the breach email again: her old phone-backup account had leaked, contacts included. "So every number I've saved is out there," she told her roommate Manjula.
She worked in order. First she wrote one short message: "My contacts were leaked. If anyone texts asking for money or an OTP in my name, don't reply. Call me on this number." Second, she sent it to the family group and the class group. Third, she rang Nani, who never reads texts, and repeated it slowly twice. Manjula forwarded the same warning to everyone on their floor.
Two days later Mausi called, half laughing. "Someone wrote 'Sarita here, urgent, send money now.' I just phoned you instead."

qa.q: Who did Sarita phone because that person never reads texts?
qa.a: She rang Nani, who never reads texts, and repeated the warning slowly twice.

qa.q: Why did the leak worry Sarita so much?
qa.a: She felt alarmed because every number she had saved was out there, so the people she loves could be the next targets.

qa.q: What else could Sarita set up so relatives know what to do?
qa.a: She could agree one simple check with the family, like always calling her back on her known number, so any strange request gets tested before anyone acts.

qa.q: How did the warning look from Mausi's side two days later?
qa.a: For Mausi, a scary 'urgent' text became almost funny, because she already knew to phone Sarita instead of replying.

grounding: Shows the person warning relatives and friends in clear steps to ignore messages asking for money or OTPs after a contact list leaked.

Dear Jaya Bua,
Please read this before you open any other messages today.
The coaching centre I joined in June wrote to say its student records were leaked. That includes the emergency contacts we filled in, which means your number and Papa's.
So, three things:
1. If anyone messages or calls saying I'm in trouble and need money, don't send anything. Call me on my usual number first.
2. Never share an OTP with anyone, even if they say they're from the bank or the centre.
3. Could you explain this to Dadi when you visit? She trusts every caller.
I've already told Papa and Chachu. Chachu got a strange text yesterday asking for a "fee transfer" in my name, and he just deleted it, so the warning is working.
Sorry for the worry.
Urmila

qa.q: Whose numbers were on the coaching centre's emergency contact list?
qa.a: Jaya Bua's number and Papa's were on it.

qa.q: What might Urmila be worried about while writing?
qa.a: Urmila is anxious that someone could pose as a student in trouble and trick Jaya Bua or Dadi into sending money or sharing an OTP.

qa.q: What else could make Urmila's warning even stronger?
qa.a: Agreeing a family code word or always calling back on the usual number gives everyone one clear test instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Jaya Bua feel reading the email?
qa.a: Jaya Bua might feel a little uneasy but also trusted, since the email gives clear steps and asks her help in explaining things to Dadi.

grounding: Shows the person alerting relatives, whose numbers were part of the leak, to ignore messages asking for money or OTPs.
